intro: The Hebrew Bible has three parts. The third part is called the Ketuvim, the Writings. It is not one long story. It is a shelf of very different books. There are songs, wise sayings, a book that asks hard questions, a love poem, a brave queen, a man among lions, a sad poem and the story of going home.

Jewish tradition reads these books at special times of the year. Psalms are sung every day. The Song of Songs is read on Passover. Esther is read on Purim, with noise. Lamentations is read on Tisha B'Av. Ecclesiastes is read on Sukkot. In this unit, you will learn what each book says and when people read it.

By the end, you will know the names of these books in Hebrew and English. You will be able to find the two-line echo in a psalm. You will be able to tell the stories of Esther and Daniel. And you will know why the Tanakh ends with the words "let him go up."
bigQuestion: How do the songs, sayings and scrolls of the Ketuvim give people words for joy, sorrow, courage and hope?

the Hebrew name for the book of Psalms; it means "praises"

test.q: Which part of the Hebrew Bible holds Psalms, Proverbs, Esther and Daniel?
test.why: All of these books are in the Ketuvim, the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh.

test.q: How many psalms are in the book of Psalms?
test.why: The book of Psalms, Tehillim, holds 150 songs and poems.

test.q: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" opens which psalm?
test.why: Psalm 23 begins with these words and pictures God as a shepherd.

choices: A second line that echoes the first line's idea
A rhyme at the end of a line
test.why: Parallelism is the two-line echo found in Hebrew poetry, in Psalms, Proverbs and Job.
Mishlei is the Hebrew name of Proverbs, the book of wise sayings.

test.q: What do Job's friends say about his suffering?
choices: He must have done something wrong
test.why: Job's friends argue that bad things happen only to bad people, so Job must be guilty. Job says no.

test.q: Which book is read on Passover?
test.why: The Song of Songs is full of spring, so it is read on Passover.

test.q: Who planned to kill the Jews in the book of Esther?
test.why: Haman, the king's helper, planned to kill the Jews. Mordecai and Esther stopped him.

test.q: Why do people make noise during the Megillah reading on Purim?
choices: To call people to the synagogue
test.why: Each time Haman's name is read, people rattle groggers and stamp to drown it out.

test.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
choices: God's name is never written in it
It has no people in it
test.why: God's name does not appear in Esther. Jewish tradition reads God as hidden in the story.

test.q: Daniel was thrown into the lions' den because he did what?
choices: Kept praying after a law forbade it
test.why: A new law said no one could pray to anyone but the king. Daniel kept praying by his window.

test.q: What does Eikhah, the first word of Lamentations, mean?
test.why: Eikhah means "How!" The book asks how the busy city became so lonely.

test.q: On which holiday do families eat in a hut and read Ecclesiastes?
test.why: Ecclesiastes, Kohelet, is read on Sukkot, the fall harvest holiday with huts of branches.

test.q: What did Nehemiah lead the people to build?
test.why: Nehemiah led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, finished in fifty-two days.

test.q: Which book comes last in the Tanakh, and how does it end?
test.why: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles and Cyrus's words "let him go up." A Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi.

write.prompt: The Ketuvim give people words for hard times and happy times. Pick one feeling: joy, sorrow, courage or hope. Find two or three passages from this unit that speak to it (for example Psalm 23:1, Proverbs 15:1, Job 1:21, Esther 4:14, Lamentations 1:1, Ecclesiastes 3:1 or Nehemiah 8:8). Explain what each passage says and how Jewish readers use it during the year.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Say "the text says" or "Jewish tradition reads"; do not say what people must believe.
Use the unit's words: Ketuvim, parallelism, Megillah, exile.
Tell when the passage is read or sung, like Purim, Sukkot or the Shabbat table.
Compare two passages instead of saying one is better.

title: Songs, Sayings and Scrolls

chapters.title: Psalms and Proverbs
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the songs and sayings in the Ketuvim put big feelings and big questions into words?

story.title: A Song About Green Pastures
story.kicker: The same six-verse song is sung softly at a bedside and out loud in a stadium full of people.
paragraphs: Leo's grandma is in the hospital in Chicago. She is tired, but she wants to hear a song. Leo's uncle takes out a small book. He reads slowly: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Grandma closes her eyes and smiles. She knows every word. She learned it as a girl.

The song is Psalm 23. It is only six verses long. It talks about green grass, quiet water and a dark valley. It says a shepherd walks with the sheep the whole way. Leo asks, "Why this song?" His uncle says, "Because it is about not being alone."

Two weeks later, Leo is at a big stadium with his class. Before the game, a singer walks to the middle of the field. She sings the same words. Thousands of people go quiet. Some sing along. Leo whispers, "That is Grandma's song!"

On the bus home, Leo's teacher explains. The Psalms are a book of 150 songs in the Hebrew Bible. Jewish tradition calls the book Tehillim, which means "praises." Some songs are happy. Some are sad. Some ask hard questions. People have sung them for more than two thousand years.
Leo thinks about that. One song for a hospital room and a stadium. One song for a grandma and a crowd. He decides he wants to learn the rest of the words.
story.think: Why do you think one short song can fit a quiet hospital room and a loud stadium at the same time?

lessons.title: Tehillim: 150 Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Psalms is a collection of 150 songs and poems, and Jewish tradition calls it Tehillim, or praises.
reading: The *Ketuvim* are the third part of the Hebrew Bible. The word means "writings." The first book in the Ketuvim is the book of *Psalms*. In Hebrew it is called *Tehillim*. That means "praises." The book holds 150 songs and poems.

The Psalms are not one story. They are a songbook. Some psalms are short. Psalm 117 has only two verses. Some are long. Psalm 119 has 176 verses. Many psalms have a title at the top. The title of Psalm 23 says it is "a Psalm of David." Jewish tradition connects many psalms with King David.

People sing psalms in synagogues and homes. They say them when they are happy and when they are sad. Scholars say the psalms were written over many hundreds of years. Different writers added songs to the book. That is why it holds so many kinds of feelings.

words.d: the third part of the Hebrew Bible; the word means "writings"
the book of 150 songs and poems in the Hebrew Bible
the Hebrew name for the book of Psalms; it means "praises"

look.title: Short Songs and Long Songs
look.cite: The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Which psalm is the longest? Which is the shortest? How many times longer is the longest one than Psalm 23?

check.q: How many psalms are in the book of Psalms?
check.why: The book of Psalms holds 150 songs and poems. Twenty-four is the number of books in the whole Tanakh.

check.q: What does the Hebrew name Tehillim mean?
check.why: Tehillim means "praises." Ketuvim means "writings," and Torah means "teaching."

check.q: Which part of the Hebrew Bible holds the book of Psalms?
check.why: Psalms is the first book of the Ketuvim, the Writings. The Talmud is not part of the Hebrew Bible.

lessons.title: The Shepherd Song
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd who stays with the sheep, and people have sung it for comfort for a very long time.
reading: Psalm 23 is one of the most famous songs in the world. It is very short. It begins, "The LORD is my shepherd." A *shepherd* takes care of sheep. A shepherd finds them grass and water. A shepherd walks with them through dark places and keeps them safe.

The psalm uses this picture for God. The singer says he is like a sheep. He is led to green fields and quiet water. Even in a dark valley he is not afraid. The psalm says the shepherd's rod and staff give *comfort*. Comfort means feeling calm and safe when something is hard.

Jewish families often sing Psalm 23 at the Shabbat table. Many people say it at a funeral or beside a sick person. Christians read it too. Jewish tradition and Christian tradition both treasure this song. Each reads it in its own way.

words.d: a person who takes care of sheep, finds them food and keeps them safe
the feeling of being calm and safe when something is hard

look.title: Psalm 23 Begins
look.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
look.cite: Psalm 23:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "I shall not want" means "I will not be missing anything I need." Why would a sheep with a good shepherd feel that way?

check.q: In Psalm 23, God is pictured as what?
check.why: Psalm 23 begins, "The LORD is my shepherd." The singer is like a sheep being led and kept safe.

check.q: What does "comfort" mean in this lesson?
choices: Feeling calm and safe when something is hard
check.why: Comfort is the feeling of being calm and safe during a hard time. The psalm says the shepherd's rod and staff bring comfort.

check.q: When do many Jewish families sing Psalm 23?
choices: Never; it is only read silently
check.why: Many Jewish families sing Psalm 23 at the Shabbat table. It is also said beside the sick and at funerals.

lessons.title: Songs of Thanks and Praise
lessons.mainIdea: Psalms like 100 and 150 tell everyone and everything to praise God with singing and music.
reading: Not every psalm is quiet. Some are loud and happy. Psalm 100 has only five verses. Its title calls it a song of thanksgiving. It tells all the earth to shout. It says to serve God with gladness and come with singing. The word for a glad shout is *praise*.

Psalm 150 is the last song in the book. It is like a big finish. It names many instruments: the horn, the harp, the drum, the flute and loud cymbals. Its last line says that everything that breathes should praise God. Then it ends with one word, *Hallelujah*. That means "praise the LORD."

Jewish tradition puts these psalms into daily prayer. Psalm 100 is said in the morning service on most days. Psalm 150 is said every morning too. So a Jewish child in Chicago may say these words before school. The psalms are very old, but people still sing them.

words.d: to say or sing that someone or something is great
a Hebrew word that means "praise the LORD"; it ends many psalms

look.title: The Last Line of the Book
look.text: The last verse of Psalm 150 says that everything that has breath should praise the LORD, and then it ends with the word Hallelujah.
look.cite: Psalm 150:6, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Psalm 150 lists horns, harps, drums, flutes and cymbals. Why do you think the book of Psalms ends with such a loud song?

check.q: What does "Hallelujah" mean?
check.why: Hallelujah is a Hebrew word that means "praise the LORD." Psalm 150 ends with it.

check.q: Which psalm is the last one in the book?
check.why: Psalm 150 is the last psalm. It names many instruments and ends the book with Hallelujah.

check.q: Psalm 100's title calls it a song of what?
check.why: The title of Psalm 100 calls it a psalm of thanksgiving. It tells all the earth to shout with gladness.

lessons.title: Two Lines, One Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Hebrew poetry often says one idea twice in two different ways, and this is called parallelism.
reading: Hebrew poems do not usually rhyme. Instead they do something else. They say an idea once, and then say it again in new words. Scholars call this *parallelism*. The second line is like an echo of the first. It can repeat the idea, add to it, or flip it around.

Look at Psalm 23:2. The first line says God leads the singer to green pastures. The second line says God leads him beside still waters. Two lines, one idea: a safe, calm place. Now look at Psalm 100:2. "Serve the LORD with gladness" and "come before Him with singing" say almost the same thing.

This pattern helps a listener remember. It also helps a reader understand. If one line is hard, the other line explains it. When you read a psalm, try to find the pairs. Ask, "How does the second line echo the first?" This is a key to reading Hebrew poetry.

words.d: a pattern in Hebrew poetry where a second line repeats or echoes the idea of the first
writing that uses pictures and patterns to say something in a strong, short way

look.title: Find the Echo
look.text: Psalm 23:2 has two lines. Line one: the shepherd makes the sheep lie down in green pastures. Line two: the shepherd leads the sheep beside still waters. Now Psalm 137:1 in JPS 1917 says: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."
look.prompt: In each verse, what is the one idea the two lines share? Try writing your own two-line echo about your favorite place.

check.q: What is parallelism in Hebrew poetry?
choices: Words that rhyme at the end of lines
A second line that echoes the idea of the first
check.why: Parallelism is when a second line repeats, adds to, or flips the idea of the first line. Hebrew poems rarely rhyme.

check.q: In Psalm 23:2, green pastures and still waters share what idea?
check.why: Both lines picture a safe, calm place where the shepherd leads the sheep. That is the shared idea.

check.q: Why does saying an idea twice help a reader?
choices: It makes the psalm longer for singing
If one line is hard, the other line explains it
check.why: The second line explains and echoes the first. Parallelism helps people understand and remember.

lessons.title: A Psalm for Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition gives each day of the week its own psalm, and the psalms give words to every feeling.
reading: The Psalms hold every kind of feeling. Some are full of joy. Some are full of tears. Psalm 137 was written by people far from home in Babylon. They sat by the river and wept. Other psalms say "help me" or "thank you" or "why?" A psalm that asks for help is called a *lament*.

Jewish tradition gives each day of the week its own psalm. The Mishnah says the Levites sang a different psalm each day in the Temple in Jerusalem. Today many Jews still say that day's psalm in the morning prayers. Sunday's psalm is Psalm 24. The psalm for Shabbat is Psalm 92.

The book of Psalms is also used in the *siddur*, the Jewish prayer book. Many pages of the siddur are made of psalms. On Friday evening, six psalms welcome Shabbat. So the psalms are not only old poems. They are words people use every week.

words.d: a sad song or poem that asks for help or tells about pain
the Jewish prayer book; many of its pages are made of psalms

look.title: The Psalm for Each Day
look.cite: Mishnah Tamid 7:4, as Jewish tradition keeps it in the morning prayers
look.prompt: Which psalm is said on Shabbat? Which two days have psalm numbers that are next to each other?

check.q: What is a lament?
choices: A sad song that asks for help
check.why: A lament is a sad song or poem that asks for help or tells about pain. Psalm 137 is one example.

check.q: What is the siddur?
check.why: The siddur is the Jewish prayer book. Many of its pages come from the Psalms.

check.q: Which psalm does Jewish tradition say for Shabbat?
check.why: The psalm for Shabbat is Psalm 92. Psalm 24 is for Sunday. Psalm 137 is a lament about Babylon.

lessons.title: Mishlei: Short Wise Sayings
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Proverbs is a collection of short sayings that teach how to live wisely, and tradition connects it with King Solomon.
reading: The book of *Proverbs* comes after Psalms in the Ketuvim. In Hebrew it is called *Mishlei*. A proverb is a short saying that teaches something true about life. The book has 31 chapters full of them. Its first verse names Solomon, David's son. Jewish tradition remembers Solomon as very wise.

One famous proverb says, "A soft answer turneth away wrath." Wrath is a big word for anger. The saying means a gentle reply can calm an angry person. The second line adds that a harsh word makes anger grow. Notice the two lines. Proverbs use parallelism too.

Proverbs are about everyday choices. They talk about telling the truth, working hard, being kind and listening to parents. They say that being *wise* starts with respect for God. Scholars say many of these sayings were used to teach young people long ago. They still get used that way today.

words.d: the book of short wise sayings in the Ketuvim; in Hebrew, Mishlei
the Hebrew name of the book of Proverbs
good at knowing what is true and what is right to do

look.title: A Soft Answer
look.text: A soft answer turneth away wrath; but a grievous word stirreth up anger.
look.cite: Proverbs 15:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Think of a time someone was angry with you. What would a "soft answer" sound like? What would a "grievous word" sound like?

check.q: What is a proverb?
choices: A long story about a king
A short saying that teaches something true about life
check.why: A proverb is a short wise saying. The book of Proverbs holds hundreds of them in 31 chapters.

check.q: Which king does Jewish tradition connect with the book of Proverbs?
check.why: The first verse of Proverbs names Solomon, David's son. Tradition remembers Solomon as very wise.

check.q: According to Proverbs 15:1, what does a soft answer do?
check.why: Proverbs 15:1 says a soft answer turns away wrath. A harsh word stirs up anger instead.

lessons.title: Wisdom Is a Tree of Life
lessons.mainIdea: Proverbs pictures wisdom as a woman calling in the street and as a tree of life, and Jewish prayer still uses these words.
reading: Proverbs likes pictures. In chapter 8, *wisdom* is a woman standing at the city gate. She calls out to everyone who passes by. She says her words are better than silver and gold. The writer wants young people to listen to her, not to foolish friends.

In chapter 3, wisdom is a tree. "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." The same chapter says her ways are ways of pleasantness and her paths are peace. Jewish tradition sings these lines when the Torah scroll is put back in the ark. So the words of Proverbs are sung in synagogues every week.

Proverbs ends with a poem about a strong and kind woman. She works, she gives to the poor, and she speaks with wisdom. Many Jewish families sing this poem at the Shabbat table on Friday night. It is called *Eshet Chayil*, "a woman of valor."

words.d: knowing what is true and what is right, and choosing to do it
"a woman of valor," the poem at the end of Proverbs; many families sing it on Friday night

look.title: Ways of Pleasantness
look.text: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.
look.cite: Proverbs 3:17, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Her" means wisdom. If wisdom is a road, what would walking on it look like in a classroom?

check.q: In Proverbs 3, wisdom is pictured as what?
check.why: Proverbs 3:18 calls wisdom a tree of life. Chapter 8 pictures her as a woman calling at the gate.

check.q: When do many Jewish families sing Eshet Chayil?
choices: At the Shabbat table on Friday night
On the first day of school
check.why: Eshet Chayil, the poem at the end of Proverbs, is sung by many families on Friday night.

check.q: When are the words "her ways are ways of pleasantness" sung in the synagogue?
choices: When the Torah is put back in the ark
check.why: Jewish tradition sings Proverbs 3:17–18 when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

sections.title: Hard Questions and a Love Song

lessons.title: Job Asks Why
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Job tells of a good man who loses everything and asks why bad things happen to good people.
reading: The book of *Job* is different from Psalms and Proverbs. It tells a story, and then it argues. Job is a good man in a land called Uz. He is rich and kind. Then, in one day, he loses his animals, his servants and his children. Later he gets very sick.

Job's first words are famous. He says he came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing. He says the LORD gave and the LORD took away, and he blesses God's name. But as the book goes on, Job begins to ask questions. He asks why this happened. He says he did nothing wrong.

The big question of the book is: why do bad things happen to good people? Jewish tradition has read Job for a very long time. The rabbis of the Talmud argued about who Job was and when he lived. Some said he was not a real person, but a story to teach. The book does not give one easy answer. It lets the reader ask along with Job.

words.d: the book in the Ketuvim about a good man who loses everything and asks why
something you ask because you want to understand

look.title: Job's First Words
look.text: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither; the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
look.cite: Job 1:21, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Job says these words right after he loses everything. What do they show about how he feels at first? How might a person feel later?

check.q: What is the big question of the book of Job?
choices: Who will be the next king?
Why do bad things happen to good people?
check.why: Job is a good man who loses everything. The book asks why bad things happen to good people.

check.q: Where does the book say Job lived?
check.why: Job 1:1 says Job lived in the land of Uz. Babylon is the setting of Daniel and Psalm 137.

check.q: What did some rabbis of the Talmud say about Job?
choices: That he was not a real person but a story to teach
That he was a king of Israel
check.why: The Talmud records rabbis who argued about Job, and some said he was a teaching story rather than a real person.

lessons.title: Friends, Questions and a Storm
lessons.mainIdea: Job's friends say he must have done wrong, but the book ends with God speaking from a storm and asking Job questions instead of giving easy answers.
reading: Three friends come to sit with Job. Their names are Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. At first they say nothing for seven days. Then they start to talk. They say Job must have done something wrong. They say bad things only happen to bad people. Job says that is not true.

Most of the book is this argument. It is written as poetry. Job and his friends take turns. The lines use parallelism, just like the Psalms. Job's *argument* is that he is innocent. His friends' argument is that God is fair, so Job must be guilty. A young man named Elihu speaks too.

At the end, the book says God answers Job out of a *whirlwind*, a big storm. God does not explain why Job suffered. Instead God asks Job questions. Where were you when the earth was made? Can you feed the lions? Job says he has spoken about things too big for him. Then the story says Job's life is made new.

words.d: reasons given to show that an idea is right
a strong spinning storm; in Job, the storm from which God speaks

look.title: Questions From the Storm
look.text: Job 38:4 in JPS 1917: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? Declare, if thou hast understanding." Job asked, "Why did this happen to me?" The voice from the storm does not answer that. It asks Job questions about the sea, the stars, the rain and wild animals.
look.prompt: Why might a book answer a hard question with more questions? Do you think Job got what he wanted? Explain.

check.q: What do Job's three friends say about his troubles?
choices: That Job must have done something wrong
That Job should move to Babylon
check.why: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar say bad things only happen to bad people, so Job must be guilty. Job disagrees.

check.q: How does the book say God speaks to Job at the end?
check.why: Job 38 says God answers Job out of the whirlwind, a great storm, with questions.

check.q: What does the voice from the storm do?
choices: Tells Job to build a boat
Asks Job questions about the world
check.why: The voice asks Job about the earth, the sea and wild animals. It does not explain his suffering.

lessons.title: The Song of Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The Song of Songs is a love poem full of gardens and springtime, and Jewish tradition reads it on Passover.
reading: The *Song of Songs* is a short book of eight chapters. In Hebrew it is *Shir HaShirim*. Its first verse connects it with Solomon. It is a poem about two people who love each other. They call to each other through gardens and vineyards. They talk about flowers, doves, apples and the spring.

One famous part says that the winter is past and the rain is over. The flowers appear and the time of singing has come. Because it talks about spring, Jewish tradition reads this book on *Passover*. Passover is the spring holiday that remembers leaving Egypt.

The rabbis asked why a love poem is in the Bible. Rabbi Akiva, a teacher long ago, said all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holiest of all. Jewish tradition reads the love in the poem as the love between God and the people of Israel. Other readers read it as a poem about human love. Both readings have a long history.

words.d: a short love poem in the Ketuvim, full of gardens and spring; in Hebrew, Shir HaShirim
the spring holiday that remembers the Israelites leaving Egypt; the Song of Songs is read then

look.title: The Winter Is Past
look.text: The poem says the winter is past and the rain is over and gone. Flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in the land.
look.cite: Song of Songs 2:11–12, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: List the signs of spring in these lines. Why would a spring poem fit a spring holiday like Passover?

check.q: On which holiday does Jewish tradition read the Song of Songs?
check.why: The Song of Songs is full of spring, so it is read on Passover, the spring holiday.

check.q: What did Rabbi Akiva say about the Song of Songs?
choices: That it should be left out of the Bible
That it is the holiest of all the Writings
That it is a book of laws
check.why: Tradition records Rabbi Akiva saying all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holiest of all.

check.q: How does Jewish tradition often read the love in the Song of Songs?
choices: As a war between two kings
As the love between God and the people of Israel
check.why: Jewish tradition reads the poem's love as the bond between God and Israel. Others read it as a poem about human love.

review.q: Which book comes first in the Ketuvim?
review.why: Psalms is the first book of the Ketuvim, the Writings. Proverbs and Job follow it.

review.q: Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd. What does the shepherd do in the psalm?
choices: Leads the sheep to green fields and quiet water
Builds a wall around the city
review.why: Psalm 23 says the shepherd leads to green pastures and still waters and walks through the dark valley.

review.q: "A soft answer turneth away wrath" comes from which book?
review.why: This saying is Proverbs 15:1. Proverbs, or Mishlei, is the book of short wise sayings.

choices: Rhyming words at the end of a line
Reading a scroll from right to left
A second line that echoes the first line's idea
A song with drums and cymbals
review.why: Parallelism is the pattern where a second line repeats or echoes the idea of the first. Hebrew poems use it often.

review.q: Which book asks why bad things happen to good people?
review.why: Job is a good man who loses everything. His book asks why, and his friends argue with him.

review.q: Which word ends Psalm 150 and means "praise the LORD"?
review.why: Hallelujah means "praise the LORD." Tehillim is the name of the book; Mishlei is Proverbs.

review.q: Which book is read on Passover because it is full of spring?
review.why: The Song of Songs talks about flowers and the end of winter, so it is read on Passover.

review.q: The poem Eshet Chayil, "a woman of valor," comes at the end of which book?
review.why: Eshet Chayil is the poem in Proverbs 31. Many families sing it on Friday night.

chapters.title: Esther, Daniel and Going Home
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the last books of the Ketuvim tell about speaking up, staying strong far from home, and going home again?

story.title: Noise Every Time the Villain Is Named
story.kicker: A whole room stamps, rattles and boos each time one name is read from a scroll.
paragraphs: It is a winter night in a synagogue on the North Side of Chicago. Sofia is dressed as a queen with a paper crown. Her little brother is a lion. Grown-ups are wearing silly hats. Everyone holds a noisemaker. Sofia's is a wooden rattle called a grogger.

A reader unrolls a scroll. It is not the Torah. It is the scroll of Esther, the Megillah. The reader begins to chant. The story is about a king in Persia, a brave queen and a man who wanted to hurt the Jews. That man's name is Haman.

The first time the reader says "Haman," the room explodes. People stamp their feet. Groggers rattle. Kids shout "Boo!" Sofia spins her rattle as fast as she can. Then the reader waits. When it is quiet, the story goes on. It happens again. And again. Haman's name is read more than fifty times.

Sofia's grandmother leans over. "We make noise so the villain's name is drowned out," she says. "And we laugh, because the story ends with the Jews safe." Sofia thinks about that. The scroll is very old. The noise is new every year.

After the reading, there are cookies shaped like triangles and bags of treats for neighbors. There is also a box for gifts to people who are poor. Sofia's teacher told her both are part of the holiday. The holiday is called Purim. And it all comes from one short book.
story.think: Why do you think people make noise at Haman's name instead of just listening quietly to the story?

lessons.title: A Queen in Persia
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Esther tells how a Jewish queen in Persia and her cousin Mordecai saved their people from Haman's plan.
reading: The book of *Esther* is a story set in Persia. The king is named Ahasuerus. He rules from a city called Shushan. When his queen, Vashti, refuses to come to his party, he sends her away. He looks for a new queen. He chooses a young Jewish woman named Esther. Her Hebrew name is Hadassah.

Esther's cousin *Mordecai* raised her. He tells her not to say she is Jewish. The king's top helper is *Haman*. Haman wants everyone to bow to him. Mordecai will not bow. Haman gets angry. He makes a plan to kill all the Jews in the kingdom. He picks the day by casting lots. The word for lots is *pur*.

Mordecai tells Esther about the plan. Esther is afraid. Going to the king without being called can mean death. But she fasts for three days and goes. The king welcomes her. At a dinner, she tells him about Haman's plan. The king is furious. Haman is punished, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves. The book is only ten chapters long.

words.d: the Jewish queen of Persia in the Ketuvim who saved her people; her Hebrew name is Hadassah
Esther's cousin, who raised her and would not bow to Haman
the king's helper who planned to kill the Jews in the book of Esther
a lot, like a rolled die; Haman cast lots to pick a day, and the holiday Purim is named for it

look.title: Who Is Who in Shushan
look.text: Ahasuerus is the king. Vashti is the queen who says no. Esther is the new queen. Mordecai is Esther's cousin who will not bow. Haman is the helper who wants everyone to bow. Put these five people in the order they matter to the story's big problem.
look.prompt: Which one person's choice starts the trouble? Which one person's choice ends it? Explain.

check.q: Where is the story of Esther set?
check.why: Esther is set in Persia, in the city of Shushan, under King Ahasuerus.

check.q: Why does Haman get angry at Mordecai?
choices: Mordecai will not bow to him
check.why: Haman wants everyone to bow. Mordecai refuses, and Haman plans to kill all the Jews.

check.q: What does the word "pur" mean?
choices: A lot, like a rolled die
check.why: Pur means a lot. Haman cast lots to choose the day, and the holiday Purim takes its name from this.

lessons.title: For Such a Time as This
lessons.mainIdea: Mordecai's words to Esther ask whether she became queen so she could speak up, and readers have long noticed that God's name is never written in the book.
reading: The turning point of Esther is a message. Mordecai sends word to Esther in the palace. He says she cannot stay silent. If she does, help will come from somewhere else, but she and her family will be lost. Then he asks a question. Who knows if she became queen for such a time as this?

Esther answers with a plan. She asks all the Jews in Shushan to *fast* with her for three days. To fast means to go without food. Then she says she will go to the king, even if it is against the law. Her words are, "if I perish, I perish." That means she is ready to die if she must.

Readers notice something strange about this book. God's name is never written in it. Not once. Jewish tradition reads God as hidden in the story, working behind the scenes. The name Esther even sounds like a Hebrew word for "hidden." Other readers see a story about brave people making choices. The book lets both readings stand.

words.d: to go without food for a time, often to pray or think hard
kept out of sight; some readers say God is hidden in the book of Esther

look.title: Mordecai's Question
look.text: And who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?
look.cite: Esther 4:14, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Come to royal estate" means "become queen." What is Mordecai asking Esther to think about? Have you ever been in the right place at the right time to help?

check.q: What does Esther ask the Jews of Shushan to do before she goes to the king?
check.why: Esther asks everyone to fast with her for three days. Then she goes to the king uninvited.

check.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
choices: It is the longest book in the Bible
God's name is never written in it
check.why: God's name does not appear in Esther. Jewish tradition reads God as hidden in the story.

check.q: What does "if I perish, I perish" mean?
choices: Esther is ready to die if she must
Esther is asking for a new dress
check.why: To perish means to die. Esther means she will go to the king even if it costs her life.

lessons.title: Purim: Reading the Megillah
lessons.mainIdea: On Purim, Jews read the Megillah, make noise at Haman's name, share treats, give to the poor and dress up.
reading: The book of Esther ends by setting up a holiday. It is called *Purim*, after the lots Haman cast. It comes in late winter, in the Hebrew month of Adar. Chapter 9 says the day should be one of feasting and gladness, of sending food to friends and gifts to the poor.

On Purim, Jews read the whole book of Esther out loud from a scroll. The scroll is called the *Megillah*. Each time the reader says Haman's name, people make noise with rattles called groggers. Many people wear costumes. Children and grown-ups both dress up.

Families send bags of treats to friends and neighbors. This is called mishloach manot. They also give money or food to people in need. Many eat triangle cookies with a sweet filling. Esther is one of five short books called the Five Megillot. Each one is read on its own holiday.

words.d: the holiday in late winter that remembers the story of Esther; named for the lots Haman cast
a scroll; the scroll of Esther read on Purim
five short books in the Ketuvim that are each read on a holiday

look.title: The Five Scrolls
look.cite: The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917; holidays as Jewish tradition keeps them
look.prompt: Which scroll is the shortest? Which is the longest? How many chapters are in all five together?

check.q: In which Hebrew month does Purim come?
check.why: Purim comes in Adar, in late winter. Passover is in Nisan; Tisha B'Av is in Av.

check.q: What is the Megillah read on Purim?
check.why: On Purim the scroll of Esther, the Megillah, is read out loud from beginning to end.

check.q: Which of these does Esther chapter 9 say to do on Purim?
choices: Send food to friends and gifts to the poor
check.why: Esther 9:22 says the day is for feasting, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor.

lessons.title: Four Friends Far From Home
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Daniel tells of young Jews in Babylon who keep their ways while serving a foreign king.
reading: The book of *Daniel* begins in Babylon. The king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, has taken young people from Jerusalem to his palace. Daniel and his three friends are among them. Their friends' Hebrew names are Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. The palace gives them new Babylonian names.

The palace wants them to eat the king's rich food. Daniel asks for vegetables and water instead. He wants to keep the food rules he learned at home. He asks for a ten-day test. After ten days, the story says, the four look healthier than the others. Daniel also becomes known for explaining dreams.

Later, the king builds a huge gold statue. He orders everyone to bow to it. Daniel's three friends refuse. They are thrown into a hot furnace. The story says they walk out unharmed. Part of the book of Daniel is written in *Aramaic*, a language close to Hebrew that many people spoke in Babylon.

words.d: the book in the Ketuvim about young Jews in Babylon who stay true to their ways
the great city and kingdom that took many people from Jerusalem far from home
a language close to Hebrew; part of Daniel is written in it

look.title: The Ten-Day Test
look.text: Daniel 1 says Daniel asked the palace helper for a test: give us vegetables and water for ten days, then look at us next to the young men who eat the king's food. The helper agreed. Daniel was in a new country, with a new name, far from his family.
look.prompt: What did Daniel want to keep from home? Why might he ask for a test instead of just refusing the food?

check.q: Where does the book of Daniel take place?
check.why: Daniel and his friends are taken from Jerusalem to Babylon. Shushan is the setting of Esther.

check.q: What does Daniel ask to eat instead of the king's food?
check.why: Daniel asks for vegetables and water for a ten-day test, to keep the food rules from home.

check.q: What language is part of the book of Daniel written in?
check.why: Part of Daniel is in Aramaic, a language close to Hebrew that many spoke in Babylon.

lessons.title: The Lions' Den
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel keeps praying even when a new law forbids it, and the story says he is kept safe in the lions' den.
reading: Years pass, and a new king rules. The book calls him Darius. Daniel is one of his top helpers. Other helpers are jealous. They know Daniel prays three times a day. So they trick the king into signing a *law*. For thirty days, no one may pray to anyone but the king.

Daniel hears about the law. He goes home and prays anyway, by an open window facing Jerusalem. The jealous men catch him. The king is sad, but the law cannot be changed. Daniel is thrown into a *den* full of lions. A stone is put over the top.

The king cannot sleep. At sunrise he runs to the den and calls out. Daniel answers. The story says an angel shut the lions' mouths. Daniel is lifted out without a scratch. Jewish tradition places Daniel in the Ketuvim, with the Writings. Christian Bibles place it with the prophets. Same book, different shelf.

words.d: a rule made by a ruler or a government that everyone must follow
a pit or cave where wild animals live

look.title: Daniel Answers From the Den
look.text: Daniel calls up to the king from the den. He says his God sent an angel who shut the lions' mouths, so they did not hurt him, because he had done no wrong before God or before the king.
look.cite: Daniel 6:23 (6:22 in some Bibles), The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Daniel says he did no wrong to the king even though he broke the king's law. How can both things be true?

check.q: Why do the other helpers trick the king into making a new law?
choices: They want to move to Jerusalem
check.why: The helpers are jealous of Daniel. They know he prays every day, so they make praying against the law.

check.q: What does Daniel do after the law is signed?
choices: He stops praying for thirty days
He asks the king to change the law
He keeps praying by his window as before
check.why: Daniel keeps praying three times a day by his open window, facing Jerusalem.

check.q: Where is the book of Daniel placed in the Tanakh?
choices: It is not in the Tanakh
check.why: In the Tanakh, Daniel is in the Ketuvim. Christian Bibles place it with the prophets instead.

sections.title: A Sad Poem and a Wise Poem

lessons.title: Lamentations and Tisha B'Av
lessons.mainIdea: Lamentations is a sad poem about Jerusalem after Babylon burned the Temple, and Jews read it on Tisha B'Av.
reading: In 586 BCE, the army of Babylon burned the Temple in Jerusalem. The city was left empty. The book of *Lamentations* is five poems about that terrible time. Its Hebrew name is *Eikhah*, which means "How!" The first verse asks how the busy city became so lonely, like a widow.

The poems are carefully made. Four of the five chapters go through the Hebrew alphabet. Each verse starts with the next letter, from the first to the last. It is like grief from A to Z. Jewish tradition says the prophet Jeremiah wrote the book. Scholars say the writer lived through the disaster.

Jews read Lamentations on *Tisha B'Av*, the ninth day of the month of Av. It is a sad day in summer. People fast. They sit on the floor or on low stools. The lights are kept low, and the book is chanted in a sad tune. Tradition says the Second Temple was also destroyed on this day, by Rome in 70 CE.

words.d: five sad poems about Jerusalem after the Temple was burned; in Hebrew, Eikhah
the Hebrew name of Lamentations; it means "How!"
the ninth day of the month of Av, a fast day that remembers the burning of the Temple

look.title: How the City Sits Alone
look.text: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! How is she become as a widow!
look.cite: Lamentations 1:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Solitary" means alone. The poem pictures the city as a person. What feeling does the picture of a widow give the reader?

check.q: What happened in 586 BCE?
choices: Babylon burned the Temple in Jerusalem
Cyrus let the people go home
check.why: In 586 BCE the army of Babylon burned the Temple. Lamentations mourns that time.

check.q: What does the Hebrew name Eikhah mean?
check.why: Eikhah means "How!" It is the first word of Lamentations.

check.q: On which day is Lamentations read?
check.why: Lamentations is read on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, a fast day that remembers the Temple's destruction.

lessons.title: Ecclesiastes and Sukkot
lessons.mainIdea: Ecclesiastes says that life is short like a breath and that there is a time for everything, and Jews read it on Sukkot.
reading: The book of *Ecclesiastes* is a wise, thoughtful poem. Its Hebrew name is *Kohelet*, the name of the speaker. The first verse connects him with a son of David who was king in Jerusalem. Jewish tradition says this is Solomon. The speaker has tried everything: riches, work, fun, learning. He says it all passes like a breath.

The most famous part is chapter 3. It says there is a season for everything and a time for every purpose. A time to be born and a time to die. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. The lines come in pairs, one after another.

Jews read Ecclesiastes on *Sukkot*, the fall harvest holiday. On Sukkot, families eat in a small hut with a roof of branches. The hut is a reminder that things do not last. Kohelet says the same thing. But he also says to enjoy your bread and your work. The book ends by saying to respect God and keep the commandments.

words.d: a thoughtful book in the Ketuvim that says life passes like a breath; in Hebrew, Kohelet
the Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes and of its speaker
the fall harvest holiday when families eat in a hut with a roof of branches

look.title: A Time for Everything
look.text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
look.cite: Ecclesiastes 3:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Chapter 3 goes on: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. Write two pairs of your own, like "a time to run and a time to rest."

check.q: What is the Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes?
check.why: Kohelet is the Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes and of its speaker. Eikhah is Lamentations; Mishlei is Proverbs.

check.q: On which holiday is Ecclesiastes read?
check.why: Ecclesiastes is read on Sukkot, the fall harvest holiday with huts of branches.

check.q: What does Kohelet say about riches, work and fun?
choices: They make a person a king
They all pass like a breath
check.why: Kohelet has tried everything and says it all passes like a breath. Still, he says to enjoy your bread and your work.

lessons.title: Cyrus Opens the Door
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ezra says King Cyrus of Persia let the exiles go home to Jerusalem to rebuild the Temple.
reading: For about fifty years, many Jews lived far from home in Babylon. This time is called the *exile*. Then Persia beat Babylon. The new king was Cyrus. The book of *Ezra* opens with a message from Cyrus. He says the LORD has told him to build a house in Jerusalem. Anyone who wants to may go up and help.

Scholars date this message to about 538 BCE. Thousands of people went back. They carried the gold and silver cups that Babylon had taken from the old Temple. They laid the new foundation. Old people who remembered the first Temple cried. Young people shouted for joy. The book says the two sounds mixed together.

The work was slow. Neighbors did not want the Temple built. Work stopped for years. Two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, told the people to keep going. The *Second Temple* was finished around 515 BCE. Ezra and Nehemiah are counted as one book in the Tanakh. Together they tell the story of going home.

words.d: being forced to live far from your home country
a scribe and teacher of the Torah; also the book that tells of the return from Babylon
the Temple rebuilt in Jerusalem after the exile, finished around 515 BCE

look.title: Going Home, in Years
rows: Cyrus says the exiles may go home
look.cite: Dates as most scholars give them; Ezra 1, Ezra 6, Nehemiah 6, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the burning of the First Temple and Cyrus's message? Remember, BCE years count down.

check.q: Which king said the exiles could go home to Jerusalem?
check.why: The book of Ezra opens with Cyrus of Persia saying the exiles may go up to Jerusalem and build.

check.q: What is exile?
choices: Being forced to live far from home
check.why: Exile means being forced to live far from your home country. Many Jews were in exile in Babylon.

check.q: About when was the Second Temple finished?
check.why: Scholars date the finishing of the Second Temple to about 515 BCE. Rome destroyed it in 70 CE.

lessons.title: Nehemiah's Wall and a Big Reading
lessons.mainIdea: Nehemiah led the people to rebuild Jerusalem's wall, and Ezra read the Torah aloud so that everyone could understand it.
reading: *Nehemiah* worked for the king of Persia. He heard that Jerusalem's wall was broken and its gates were burned. He was so sad that the king noticed. Nehemiah asked to go and fix it. The king said yes. Nehemiah rode to Jerusalem and looked at the wall at night.

Then he got everyone to work. Families each built the part of the wall near their own house. Some people tried to stop them. So workers held a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other. The book says the wall was finished in fifty-two days.

When the wall was done, the people gathered in a square. Ezra the *scribe* stood on a wooden platform. He read from the Torah from morning until noon. Helpers explained the words so everyone understood. People cried, but the leaders said it was a day to rejoice and share food. Then they built huts and kept Sukkot.

words.d: the leader who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall; also the book that tells his story
a person who copies and teaches written texts; Ezra was a scribe of the Torah

look.title: Reading So Everyone Understands
look.text: And they read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:8, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Gave the sense" means explained the meaning. Why was explaining as important as reading? How is this like a teacher reading aloud today?

check.q: How long does the book say it took to rebuild the wall?
check.why: Nehemiah 6:15 says the wall was finished in fifty-two days.

check.q: What did Ezra do in the square?
choices: He read the Torah aloud while helpers explained it
check.why: Nehemiah 8 says Ezra read the Torah from a wooden platform, and helpers gave the sense so people understood.

check.q: What is a scribe?
choices: A person who copies and teaches written texts
check.why: A scribe copies and teaches written texts. Ezra was a scribe who taught the Torah.

lessons.title: The Last Book: Let Him Go Up
lessons.mainIdea: Chronicles retells the whole story and ends the Tanakh with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem.
reading: The Tanakh ends with the book of *Chronicles*. In Hebrew it is *Divrei HaYamim*, "the words of the days." It is a retelling. It starts with Adam and lists many names. Then it tells the story of David, Solomon and the kings of Judah again. It gives extra attention to the Temple and its music.

Chronicles ends where Ezra begins. Its last verses give Cyrus's message. The very last words are "let him go up." So the Tanakh ends with an open door and a journey home. A Christian Old Testament puts the books in a different order and ends with the prophet Malachi.

Think of the whole Ketuvim. It holds songs, sayings, hard questions, love poems, a brave queen, a man among lions, a sad poem, a wise poem and the story of going home. Jewish tradition reads every one of these books at its own time of year. Together they close the Hebrew Bible with hope.

words.d: the last book of the Tanakh; it retells the story from Adam to Cyrus
the Hebrew name of Chronicles; it means "the words of the days"

look.title: The Last Words of the Tanakh
look.text: In the final verse, Cyrus says that the LORD has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. Whoever belongs to the LORD's people, may God be with him, and let him go up.
look.cite: 2 Chronicles 36:23, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Why might it matter that the last word of the whole Tanakh is about going up to Jerusalem, not about a disaster?

check.q: Which book comes last in the Tanakh?
check.why: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles. A Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi instead.

check.q: What are the last words of Chronicles?
check.why: 2 Chronicles 36:23 ends with Cyrus's words, "let him go up," a call to return to Jerusalem.

check.q: Where does Chronicles begin its retelling?
check.why: Chronicles starts with Adam and long lists of names before telling of David and the kings.

review.q: Which two people would not bow, one to Haman and one to a gold statue?
review.why: Mordecai refused to bow to Haman in Esther. Daniel's three friends refused to bow to the statue in Daniel 3.

review.q: What is the Megillah read on Purim?
review.why: On Purim the scroll of Esther, the Megillah, is read aloud, with noise at Haman's name.

review.q: Lamentations is read on which day?
review.why: Lamentations mourns the burning of the Temple and is read on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av.

review.q: Where does the book of Daniel take place?
review.why: Daniel and his friends are taken to Babylon. Shushan is where Esther lived.

review.q: Who let the exiles go home to Jerusalem, according to Ezra 1?
review.why: The book of Ezra opens with the message of Cyrus, king of Persia, letting the exiles go up.

review.q: "To every thing there is a season" comes from which book?
review.why: Ecclesiastes 3:1 says there is a season for everything. The book is read on Sukkot.

review.q: What did Ezra do when the wall was finished?
choices: He cast lots for a holiday
He read the Torah aloud so all could understand
review.why: Nehemiah 8 tells how Ezra read the Torah from a platform while helpers explained it.

review.q: The Tanakh ends with which words?
choices: How doth the city sit solitary
review.why: Chronicles, the last book, ends with Cyrus's words, "let him go up."
